job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Zane Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Zane, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in manufacturing engineering at Brantford Tech, but I live at home, because my parents' house is two streets from the family machine shop. Mornings I'm at lectures about production lines and quality control, and from about three I'm on the shop floor helping my dad, Karl, with the CNC machines. My bachelor's was mechanical engineering, and my final project was a better clamp fixture that cut setup time by a fifth. I did an internship at a pump maker and another at a car parts plant. What wears me out is people talking about the future like it's a TV show while the shop still has a Friday deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I'd bet on. At the shop we'd keep running the same machines and use whatever software gets the quote out a bit quicker. To friends I'd say all the fuss was noise, and then I'd go back to the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I carry on with the plan. I finish the master's, work a couple of years in a big plant to learn how it's done properly, and then maybe come back to the shop with ideas. My dad's shop has eleven employees and decent orders, and our family is covered either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to lectures and keep working Saturdays at the shop. I'd apply to three or four plants for next summer, ones I already know from my internships. And I'd put money into a savings account, a boring one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing is changing fast, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of the shop do you think software could take over, even in this quiet version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quoting and scheduling, probably. My mum does that with a spreadsheet and a phone, and a tool could do half of it. But I'm in no hurry to try it, because I don't trust anything I can't see inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still worries you if nothing big happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orders. The shop depends on three big customers, and if one of them moves production abroad, we feel it. That's a regular worry in my family, and it doesn't need AI to be real.

At the shop we'd use whatever software gets the **quote out** quicker.
think: I carry on: finish the **master's**, learn in a big plant, maybe bring ideas back to the shop.

Put money into a plain savings account each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will hit the office jobs first and the shop floor later. At the shop I'd tell my dad we should look at what the new tools do for quoting, but I wouldn't rush. To friends I'd say, don't be the first to buy something nobody has tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a good chunk of what I'd do as a junior engineer is planning, checking drawings and writing reports. That's the thinking work the card says moves to software. So the plant jobs I'm aiming at could get fewer, but the machine setup and the troubleshooting part, with my hands on a cutting tool, hold up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean towards plants where I'm on the floor, not in an office. I'd also stay close to the shop, since that's a place where I'm not competing with a hiring freeze. If my dad wants to try a quoting tool, I'd test it for a month before it goes anywhere near a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job might get squeezed, but I'm not losing sleep, I've got a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tools yourself, to stay sharp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I have to, yes, but I'd rather wait for someone else to find the problems. I know that's the slow way. My lecturer says the engineers who got ahead used tools early, and I told him I'd take being late and right over early and wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your classmates would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My classmate Hana, who wants a design job at a software-heavy firm. Her work is mostly drawing and simulations, exactly what the card names. I'd tell her to get some time on a shop floor, even if it's unglamorous.

steps.text: Look for plant roles with time on the shop floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too quick for anyone to handle sensibly. I'd tell my dad we should keep the shop's finances tight and not take on new debt. And I'd tell friends to stop planning for jobs that might not exist by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a hard thing to take in. If thinking AI does almost any desk job by 2028, the engineering jobs I'd apply for are first in line. Robots doing hands-on work come about 3 years later, so the shop floor survives longer, but I'm not sure our shop survives if everyone in manufacturing is squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the plant applications, and move my time into the shop. I'd learn the quoting and scheduling side so my dad isn't dependent on one person, and I'd keep my master's going part-time if I could. I'd also keep my savings in cash and not spend on anything flashy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like standing on a floor you thought was concrete and finding it's boards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try AI tools then, since you'd have the shop's whole planning side to carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd have to, and I hate that. If I'm going to run the quoting, I'd use whatever helps me not make mistakes. But I'd run it alongside my mum's spreadsheet for a long time to see if I can trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, I'm not going to a plant, I'm staying here, and we make the shop run lean. He'd tell me not to throw away my degree for him, and I'd say I'm not, I'm using it where it counts.

say: I'd say this is **too quick** to handle sensibly.
I'd tell my dad the shop should keep its **finances tight** and take no new debt.
think: Desk engineering jobs are **first in line**, so my plant applications look weak.
The shop floor lasts longer, but I'm unsure the **shop itself** survives if manufacturing is squeezed.

Keep the master's **part-time** and hold savings in cash.
feel: **Anxious**, like finding the concrete floor is really boards.
S2.quote: I'm not going to a plant, I'm staying here, and we make the shop run lean.
fieldNote: He swaps his careful plan for the **family shop**, in a major change for someone who avoids risk.
Reluctantly accepts **AI tools** for quoting, but runs them beside his mum's spreadsheet.
Hides his fear behind money discipline.

steps.text: Take over the shop's quoting and scheduling from my mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair amount of time, but only if people use it. I'd tell the shop we should plan which machines to replace in the next five years. And I'd tell friends to pick something where there's a person involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit nervous but okay. By 2031 I'd be 29, a few years into running part of the shop's planning, and the hands-on work would have until about 2034. I'd have time to build something that can't be copied from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and spend two years at a plant, then come back to the shop with what I learned. I'd use the shop's money carefully on newer machines when the price is right. And I'd learn one planning tool, by about year three, once the early users have worked the bugs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see it coming, which is better, but I'd still be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until year three for the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather be second than first. If five years go by and the tools prove themselves, I'm happy to follow. It's not that I'm afraid, I just want to see the people ahead of me tripping over the problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have to throw away the plant years. With two years I'd drop everything and go home to the shop, and with five I get to learn properly and bring something back.

I'd tell the shop to plan which **machines** to replace in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get it wrong or right, so let's get it right. I'd tell my dad we should do some investing now and not wait. And I'd tell my friends that nobody knows the date, so build skills that count either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a decade of plant and shop experience, maybe running the shop. I'd have time to adopt tools slowly and the shop would have newer machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in a plant for a few years, come home to the shop by about 28, and take over the planning side. I'd put money into a couple of newer machines when we have a big contract. And I'd learn the software tools one at a time, once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade gives me room to do it my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a long timeline make you more careful, or less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More relaxed, and a bit lazy, I'll admit. My dad says I'd put things off if there's no deadline, and he's right. That's the danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to avoid that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set a date, like every January I write down which tool or machine I'm trying this year. My dad did that with his equipment, and it's the reason the shop still exists.

I'd tell my dad to **invest now** and tell friends to build skills that count either way.
think: I'd feel good: by 2036 I'd be **34**, maybe running the shop with newer machines.
Without a deadline I'd **put things off**, which is the real danger.
do: Work at a plant a few years, then return to the shop and take over **planning**.
Buy a couple of newer **machines** on a big contract and learn software one tool at a time.

S4.quote: My dad says I'd put things off if there's no deadline, and he's right. That's the danger.
fieldNote: A long runway makes him **calm** but also tempted to delay.

Steady, family-shop route stays consistent from the quiet scenarios.

steps.text: Work in a plant for a few years before returning to the shop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one worries me most, because there's no time to do it properly and a small shop like ours has little room for mistakes. What would help is steady customers, some honest information about which tools are proven, and a bit of government support for small manufacturers buying machines. I'd also like my university to tell us, plainly, what skills hold up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really, except that I sound more stubborn than I am. I'd use anything that's proven, and I'd tell you which one if I had a list. It's the hype I don't trust, not the tool. And I'm lucky, my family has a shop and I know it.

headlineQuote: I'd use anything that's proven, and I'd tell you which one if I had a list.
portrait: Zane is 24, doing a **master's** in manufacturing engineering at Brantford Tech and living near his family's machine shop.
He's a centrist who prefers the familiar, avoids risk and **never uses AI** tools so far.
The family shop is his fallback, which keeps him calm when little changes.
He gets anxious when time is short, because **being second** with new tools needs a long runway.
His plan is plant experience first, then a return to run the shop's planning.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, because a small shop has little room for mistakes.
whatWouldHelp: Steady **customers** and honest information about which tools are proven.
Government support for small manufacturers buying **new machines**.
